  "title": "CRADE: Joint Contamination-Ability Decomposition via Gated Item Response Theory with Paired Adversarial Items",
  "core_problem": "No existing framework can determine whether a model fails adversarial benchmark variants because it memorized original answers (contamination) or because it lacks genuine reasoning ability (capability deficit) — all current work observes this entanglement but none models it within a measurement-theoretic framework, preventing trustworthy LLM capability assessment.",
  "opportunity": "Three previously siloed research streams — IRT-based LLM evaluation (PSN-IRT AAAI 2026 Oral, ATLAS, LEGO-IRT), contamination detection/correction (DCR EMNLP 2025, ConStat NeurIPS 2024, JECS arXiv May 2026), and adversarial robustness testing (MaSTer, RIDE, MATH-Perturb ICML 2025) — have each matured independently to the point where their integration is both technically feasible and urgently needed. The critical catalyst is Wang et al.'s ICLR 2026 proof that all likelihood-based contamination detection fails on reasoning models (AUROC ≈ 50%), creating demand for response-pattern-based alternatives that bypass token-probability signals entirely. A key theoretical precedent exists but has never been applied to LLMs: the Deterministic Gated IRT model (DGM; Shu, Henson & Luecht, Psychometrika 2013) decomposes test performance into genuine ability and cheating/preknowledge components conditioned on item exposure status — precisely the structure needed for LLM contamination. PSN-IRT showed IRT works for LLMs (12 models, 41,871 items, 4PL) but left contamination-adjusted scoring as an explicit open question, flagging anomalous guessing-rate parameters as contamination indicators without providing corrected ability estimates. RankLLM (ICLR 2026) demonstrated that non-parametric difficulty-aware ranking achieves 90% human alignment with only a damping hyperparameter — but provides no contamination decomposition, producing rankings without interpretable ability vs. memorization parameters. The AAAI 2027 deadline (abstracts July 21, papers July 28, 2026) is 8 weeks out. Nobody sits at the three-way intersection of IRT estimation, contamination correction, and adversarial pairing because these communities publish at different venues (ACL/EMNLP for contamination, ICLR/NeurIPS for robustness, AAAI for psychometric evaluation, Psychometrika/JEBS for test security).",
  "landscape": "The current best contamination-to-correction pipeline is DCR (EMNLP 2025), which produces a DCR Factor via fuzzy inference across four contamination levels, achieving ~4% average error on three benchmarks — but its ad-hoc multiplicative correction Acc_adj = Acc × (1 − DCR Factor) has no measurement-theoretic justification and empirically weakens on hard tasks (r=0.66). PSN-IRT (AAAI 2026 Oral) demonstrates IRT's power for LLM evaluation using a 4PL model across 12 LLMs on 11 benchmarks (41,871 items), flagging contamination indirectly via anomalous guessing-rate parameters, but produces no contamination-adjusted ability scores; critically, PSN-IRT succeeds with only 12 models by using neural network estimation (pseudo-Siamese architecture) rather than classical MLE, establishing that neural IRT estimation is viable at small model counts. RankLLM (ICLR 2026) provides a strong non-parametric baseline: bidirectional score propagation between models and questions achieves 90% human alignment on 30 models × 35,550 questions, with remarkable stability under model removal (ρ = 0.94 even with 50% pool removed) and 0.006s convergence — but it produces difficulty-weighted rankings without any contamination modeling. RIDE (arXiv 2025) combines IRT with adversarial perturbation for math evaluation — but uses IRT only as a difficulty reward signal for RL-based question rewriting via RIDE-8B, not for joint ability-contamination estimation. JECS (arXiv May 2026) achieves formal conformal guarantees for multi-model decontamination via joint envelope conformal selection, but wastes information by binarizing items into keep/discard rather than producing continuous corrected scores. ConStat (NeurIPS 2024) detects contamination via performance gaps on rephrased samples using a statistical comparison against reference models, but does not model it as a latent variable within a psychometric framework. In psychometrics, the DGM (Shu et al., Psychometrika 2013) uses a gated IRT formulation estimated via hierarchical MCMC to decompose examinee performance into genuine ability and item-preknowledge components — but assumes item exposure status is known a priori, which is unavailable for LLM training data. Two paired-item approaches exist but use no IRT: PaCoST (arXiv 2024) performs paired confidence significance testing for binary contamination detection, and ConStat compares primary vs. reference benchmark performance — both confirm the paired-item signal is informative but neither models it as a latent variable. For adversarial variant generation, MaSTer (arXiv 2026) provides a validated multi-round rewrite-verify pipeline (5 parallel streams × 3 iterations) achieving 45-94% target failure rates on GSM8K and MATH-500 using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and SymPy verification; code is claimed at github.com/sustech-nlp/MaSTer but was unavailable as of May 2026 — backup pipelines exist via MathCheck (ICLR 2025, open code) and MATH-Perturb (ICML 2025, 279 expert-crafted perturbations with open code). MathArena (NeurIPS 2025 D&B Track) has expanded to ~900 problems across 2025-2026 competitions (AIME 2026, HMMT Feb 2026, USAMO 2026, ArXivMath monthly, BrokenArxiv, ArXivLean, Visual Math, Project Euler, Apex) with 50+ models, providing rich uncontaminated ground-truth rankings. Recent IRT estimation advances for small samples include Fox (2025, JEBS) demonstrating IRT-BCSM for N=50-100 by analytically integrating out person parameters, and Bayesian hierarchical priors achieving stable 2PL estimation at small sample sizes. Concurrent work search (arXiv, OpenReview, May 2026): no paper attempts joint IRT-based contamination-ability decomposition with paired adversarial items — the three-way intersection remains unoccupied.",
  "inspired_by": "Field guide gaps: 'Contamination-aware IRT' (gap 3), 'Joint contamination-robustness decomposition' (gap 1); Innovation patterns: 'Self-Referential Measurement' (model as own control via original-vs-variant), 'Formal Guarantees on Evaluation Methodology' (identifiability proof for Gated-2PL), 'Detection-to-Correction Bridge' (from detection signals to calibrated ability scores); Key theoretical bridge: DGM (Shu et al. 2013) provides the gated IRT structure for item preknowledge estimated via hierarchical MCMC, which we extend to the LLM contamination setting where item exposure status is unknown but inferred from paired adversarial items; Untried combinations: 'DGM-style gated IRT with adversarial variant generation for LLM evaluation' (primary), 'Conformal p-values as contamination priors for gated IRT' (secondary), 'RankLLM non-parametric ranking as sanity-check baseline for IRT-corrected rankings' (tertiary)",
  "approach": "We extend the Deterministic Gated IRT model (DGM; Shu et al., Psychometrika 2013) from the test-security domain to LLM contamination assessment, introducing the Gated-2PL (G-2PL) model as the primary framework where correct-response probability decomposes into ability-driven and contamination-driven components via a gating mechanism. The key innovation over DGM is that item exposure status is not assumed known but is identified from paired adversarial items.

**Model specification (primary: Gated-2PL):**
- For variant item i*: P(Y_{j,i*}=1 | θ_j) = σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i − δ_i)), a standard 2PL with difficulty shift δ_i
- For original item i: P(Y_{j,i}=1 | θ_j, ξ_j, η_i) = ξ_j·η_i + (1−ξ_j·η_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i))
- θ_j = model j's genuine reasoning ability (person parameter)
- ξ_j ∈ [0,1] = model j's contamination exposure (person parameter)
- η_i ∈ [0,1] = item i's contamination susceptibility (item parameter)
- a_i, b_i = discrimination and difficulty (shared across original-variant pairs)
- δ_i = variant difficulty shift (estimated from variant calibration)

**Rationale for G-2PL over G-3PL:** The guessing parameter c_i in 3PL requires 200+ examinees for stable estimation under classical methods, while we have only 15-20 models. Dropping c_i to use 2PL eliminates the most problematic parameter for small samples while retaining the core contamination decomposition. PSN-IRT succeeded with 12 models using neural estimation, but their 4PL worked because they had 41,871 items providing massive per-item information; our gated model adds M+K contamination parameters, making parsimony critical. For math benchmarks with open-ended answers (MATH-500, GSM8K), guessing probability is effectively zero, making 2PL substantively appropriate.

**Ablation to Gated-3PL (G-3PL):**
- P(Y_{j,i*}=1 | θ_j) = c_i + (1−c_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i − δ_i))
- P(Y_{j,i}=1 | θ_j, ξ_j, η_i) = ξ_j·η_i + (1−ξ_j·η_i)·[c_i + (1−c_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i))]
- c_i fixed to domain-specific constants: c_i = 0 for open-ended math (MATH-500, GSM8K), enabling estimation only for any future MCQ extensions.

**Estimation strategy (fully specified):**
Primary: Bayesian MCMC via NumPyro/Stan with hierarchical priors, following DGM's original estimation framework:
- θ_j ~ N(0, σ²_θ), σ_θ ~ Half-Cauchy(0, 2.5)
- ξ_j ~ Beta(α_ξ, β_ξ), with α_ξ, β_ξ ~ Gamma(2, 1) (hierarchical; allows posterior to concentrate near 0 for clean models or near 1 for heavily contaminated ones)
- η_i ~ Beta(α_η, β_η), with α_η, β_η ~ Gamma(2, 1) (hierarchical)
- a_i ~ LogNormal(0, 0.5) (positive discrimination, weakly informative)
- b_i ~ N(0, 1) (centered difficulty)
- δ_i ~ N(0, 0.5) (variant shifts expected small)
- MCMC: 4 chains × 2,000 warmup + 2,000 samples, NUTS sampler, R̂ < 1.05 convergence criterion
Comparison: Neural estimation extending PSN-IRT's pseudo-Siamese architecture with an additional gating head that outputs (ξ_j, η_i) — trained via binary cross-entropy on the joint original+variant response matrix. This provides a non-Bayesian point estimate comparison.
Ablation: Variational inference via Pyro SVI as a faster alternative to MCMC, using amortized inference for scalability testing.

**Formal identifiability (central theoretical contribution):**
We prove identifiability via a two-step argument: (1) Variant items serve as contamination-free anchors, identifying θ_j and item parameters {a_i, b_i} via standard 2PL identifiability conditions (≥2 items with heterogeneous discriminations; cf. Maris & Bechger 2009). The difficulty shift δ_i is estimated from the variant calibration. (2) Given identified θ_j and item parameters, the original-variant performance gap identifies the bilinear product ξ_j·η_i. Under the rank-1 bilinear decomposition ξ_j·η_i with M models and K items, we have M·K observed gaps constraining M+K−1 free parameters (one fixed for scale), identifiable when M·K > M+K−1, i.e., (M−1)(K−1) > 0. This holds for any M,K ≥ 2. The 2PL formulation avoids the flat-likelihood surfaces that plague 3PL/4PL estimation with few examinees, as the Fisher information matrix for the 2PL is well-conditioned even at M=15.

**Bilinear rank-1 model adequacy plan:**
The rank-1 assumption (ξ_j·η_i) treats contamination as model-global and item-global, which is a first-order approximation — in reality, contamination may be topic-dependent (e.g., a model contaminated on geometry but not algebra). We address this as follows:
(a) Compute standardized residuals r_{j,i} = (Y_{j,i} − P̂_{j,i}) / √(P̂_{j,i}(1−P̂_{j,i})) from the rank-1 fit and report the residual matrix.
(b) Compute Yen's Q3 statistic for local dependence among original items after conditioning on θ_j — systematic topic-structured residuals would indicate rank-1 insufficiency.
(c) Apply person-fit statistics (standardized log-likelihood lz*) to detect models whose original-item response patterns deviate from the G-2PL predictions, flagging potential topic-specific contamination.
(d) If structured residuals emerge, explore rank-2 extension (ξ_j·η_i → ξ_j^(1)·η_i^(1) + ξ_j^(2)·η_i^(2)) or topic-stratified estimation as explicit future work.
(e) Justification for rank-1 as starting point: LLM contamination is primarily driven by overall training data overlap (entire benchmark suites appearing in Common Crawl/web scrapes) rather than topic-selective memorization; the rank-1 model captures this dominant effect.

**Data collection (within 200 H100-hr budget):**
For ~1,000 items from MATH-500 and a GSM8K subset, we generate symbolically-verified adversarial variants. Primary pipeline: MaSTer-style multi-round rewrite-verify using Qwen3.6-27B as rewriter with SymPy answer verification (~25 H100-hrs). Backup (if MaSTer code unavailable by week 1): (a) single-round rewrite-verify pipeline with Qwen3.6-27B + SymPy checking, implementable in 2-3 days; (b) MathCheck (ICLR 2025, open code at github.com/PremiLab-Math/MathCheck) for GSM8K variants; (c) seed with MATH-Perturb's 279 expert-crafted perturbations (ICML 2025, open code at github.com/Kaffaljidhmah2/MATH-Perturb) and extend via LLM rewriting for remaining items. We collect response matrices from 15-20 models: 10 open-weight (DeepSeek-R2 32B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, GLM-5.1 754B-A40B, OLMo-2-13B, Llama-4-Maverick-17B-A400B, Mistral-Large-3, plus 2 smaller reference models) and 5-8 closed-API models (GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro). For originals, we reuse Open LLM Leaderboard per-item response data (available via HuggingFace API at huggingface.co/datasets/open-llm-leaderboard/results) where available, requiring new inference only for variant items and models not on the leaderboard (~80 H100-hrs for open-weight variant inference, ~60 H100-hrs for missing original runs). IRT fitting is negligible (<1 hr CPU for MCMC).

**Validation (three-pronged, addressing domain mismatch concern):**

(1) External ranking correlation: Kendall-τ of CRADE-corrected ability rankings vs. MathArena 2026 uncontaminated competition rankings (~900 problems, 50+ models), targeting τ ≥ 0.85 (revised from 0.90 given domain mismatch between textbook-style MATH-500/GSM8K and competition-style MathArena). Report bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Compare against: (a) raw accuracy rankings, (b) RankLLM difficulty-weighted rankings, (c) DCR-corrected rankings (r=0.66 on hard tasks), (d) JECS-filtered rankings.

(2) Synthetic contamination injection (causal validation): Deliberately fine-tune OLMo-2-13B on MATH-500 training items (1 epoch, mild contamination following established protocols from contamination survey literature) and re-evaluate. If G-2PL correctly recovers elevated ξ for the fine-tuned model while θ remains stable (matching pre-contamination ability), this provides causal evidence that the decomposition works. Compare fine-tuned ξ against clean OLMo-2-13B ξ via posterior credible interval separation. This is the strongest validation because it provides ground-truth contamination status.

(3) Convergent validity with existing detectors: Correlate G-2PL's per-model ξ_j estimates with: (a) ConStat contamination flags (performance gap on rephrased vs. original), (b) PaCoST binary contamination verdicts (paired confidence significance test), (c) PSN-IRT's anomalous guessing-rate parameters. High concordance validates that ξ captures the same construct; low concordance would require investigation of what ξ uniquely captures beyond existing methods.

(4) Ablation showing differential correction benefit: Demonstrate that CRADE correction improves ranking accuracy (vs. MathArena) more for models with high estimated ξ (provably or detectably contaminated) than for models with low ξ. This confirms the correction is targeted rather than uniformly applied.

**Anchor assumption validation (variant contamination-free):**
(a) Fit standard 2PL to variant-only response matrix and compute item-fit statistics (S-X² or Orlando-Thissen) and person-fit statistics (lz*). Good fit supports the anchor assumption — variants behave like clean IRT items measuring genuine ability.
(b) Check that variant difficulty b_i + δ_i is predictable from original difficulty b_i plus a systematic shift; high-residual outlier items may indicate re-contaminated variants and should be flagged for manual review.
(c) Cross-validation: Hold out 20% of variant items, fit 2PL on remaining 80%, predict held-out responses. Prediction accuracy comparable to full-data fit supports generalizability.
(d) Ablation: Compare CRADE results using MATH-Perturb's expert-crafted perturbations (strongest anchor assumption) vs. MaSTer/LLM-generated variants to assess sensitivity to variant quality.

Ablations: (a) G-2PL vs. G-3PL (with fixed c_i = 0 for math), (b) Bayesian MCMC vs. neural estimation vs. variational inference, (c) number of variant items (100/500/1000), (d) number of models (10/15/20), (e) sensitivity to variant difficulty shift δ_i, (f) rank-1 vs. rank-2 bilinear decomposition if residuals warrant it, (g) RankLLM vs. G-2PL ranking quality.",

## Original idea
{
  "title": "CRADE: Joint Contamination-Ability Decomposition via Gated Item Response Theory with Paired Adversarial Items",
  "core_problem": "No existing framework can determine whether a model fails adversarial benchmark variants because it memorized original answers (contamination) or because it lacks genuine reasoning ability (capability deficit) — all current work observes this entanglement but none models it within a measurement-theoretic framework, preventing trustworthy LLM capability assessment.",
  "opportunity": "Three previously siloed research streams — IRT-based LLM evaluation (PSN-IRT AAAI 2026 Oral, ATLAS, LEGO-IRT), contamination detection/correction (DCR EMNLP 2025, ConStat NeurIPS 2024, JECS arXiv May 2026), and adversarial robustness testing (MaSTer, RIDE, MATH-Perturb ICML 2025) — have each matured independently to the point where their integration is both technically feasible and urgently needed. The critical catalyst is Wang et al.'s ICLR 2026 proof that all likelihood-based contamination detection fails on reasoning models (AUROC ≈ 50%), creating demand for response-pattern-based alternatives that bypass token-probability signals entirely. A key theoretical precedent exists but has never been applied to LLMs: the Deterministic Gated IRT model (DGM; Shu, Henson & Luecht, Psychometrika 2013) decomposes test performance into genuine ability and cheating/preknowledge components conditioned on item exposure status — precisely the structure needed for LLM contamination. PSN-IRT showed IRT works for LLMs (12 models, 41,871 items, 4PL) but left contamination-adjusted scoring as an explicit open question, flagging anomalous guessing-rate parameters as contamination indicators without providing corrected ability estimates. RankLLM (ICLR 2026) demonstrated that non-parametric difficulty-aware ranking achieves 90% human alignment with only a damping hyperparameter — but provides no contamination decomposition, producing rankings without interpretable ability vs. memorization parameters. The AAAI 2027 deadline (abstracts July 21, papers July 28, 2026) is 8 weeks out. Nobody sits at the three-way intersection of IRT estimation, contamination correction, and adversarial pairing because these communities publish at different venues (ACL/EMNLP for contamination, ICLR/NeurIPS for robustness, AAAI for psychometric evaluation, Psychometrika/JEBS for test security).",
  "landscape": "The current best contamination-to-correction pipeline is DCR (EMNLP 2025), which produces a DCR Factor via fuzzy inference across four contamination levels, achieving ~4% average error on three benchmarks — but its ad-hoc multiplicative correction Acc_adj = Acc × (1 − DCR Factor) has no measurement-theoretic justification and empirically weakens on hard tasks (r=0.66). PSN-IRT (AAAI 2026 Oral) demonstrates IRT's power for LLM evaluation using a 4PL model across 12 LLMs on 11 benchmarks (41,871 items), flagging contamination indirectly via anomalous guessing-rate parameters, but produces no contamination-adjusted ability scores; critically, PSN-IRT succeeds with only 12 models by using neural network estimation (pseudo-Siamese architecture) rather than classical MLE, establishing that neural IRT estimation is viable at small model counts. RankLLM (ICLR 2026) provides a strong non-parametric baseline: bidirectional score propagation between models and questions achieves 90% human alignment on 30 models × 35,550 questions, with remarkable stability under model removal (ρ = 0.94 even with 50% pool removed) and 0.006s convergence — but it produces difficulty-weighted rankings without any contamination modeling. RIDE (arXiv 2025) combines IRT with adversarial perturbation for math evaluation — but uses IRT only as a difficulty reward signal for RL-based question rewriting via RIDE-8B, not for joint ability-contamination estimation. JECS (arXiv May 2026) achieves formal conformal guarantees for multi-model decontamination via joint envelope conformal selection, but wastes information by binarizing items into keep/discard rather than producing continuous corrected scores. ConStat (NeurIPS 2024) detects contamination via performance gaps on rephrased samples using a statistical comparison against reference models, but does not model it as a latent variable within a psychometric framework. In psychometrics, the DGM (Shu et al., Psychometrika 2013) uses a gated IRT formulation estimated via hierarchical MCMC to decompose examinee performance into genuine ability and item-preknowledge components — but assumes item exposure status is known a priori, which is unavailable for LLM training data. Two paired-item approaches exist but use no IRT: PaCoST (arXiv 2024) performs paired confidence significance testing for binary contamination detection, and ConStat compares primary vs. reference benchmark performance — both confirm the paired-item signal is informative but neither models it as a latent variable. For adversarial variant generation, MaSTer (arXiv 2026) provides a validated multi-round rewrite-verify pipeline (5 parallel streams × 3 iterations) achieving 45-94% target failure rates on GSM8K and MATH-500 using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and SymPy verification; code is claimed at github.com/sustech-nlp/MaSTer but was unavailable as of May 2026 — backup pipelines exist via MathCheck (ICLR 2025, open code) and MATH-Perturb (ICML 2025, 279 expert-crafted perturbations with open code). MathArena (NeurIPS 2025 D&B Track) has expanded to ~900 problems across 2025-2026 competitions (AIME 2026, HMMT Feb 2026, USAMO 2026, ArXivMath monthly, BrokenArxiv, ArXivLean, Visual Math, Project Euler, Apex) with 50+ models, providing rich uncontaminated ground-truth rankings. Recent IRT estimation advances for small samples include Fox (2025, JEBS) demonstrating IRT-BCSM for N=50-100 by analytically integrating out person parameters, and Bayesian hierarchical priors achieving stable 2PL estimation at small sample sizes. Concurrent work search (arXiv, OpenReview, May 2026): no paper attempts joint IRT-based contamination-ability decomposition with paired adversarial items — the three-way intersection remains unoccupied.",
  "inspired_by": "Field guide gaps: 'Contamination-aware IRT' (gap 3), 'Joint contamination-robustness decomposition' (gap 1); Innovation patterns: 'Self-Referential Measurement' (model as own control via original-vs-variant), 'Formal Guarantees on Evaluation Methodology' (identifiability proof for Gated-2PL), 'Detection-to-Correction Bridge' (from detection signals to calibrated ability scores); Key theoretical bridge: DGM (Shu et al. 2013) provides the gated IRT structure for item preknowledge estimated via hierarchical MCMC, which we extend to the LLM contamination setting where item exposure status is unknown but inferred from paired adversarial items; Untried combinations: 'DGM-style gated IRT with adversarial variant generation for LLM evaluation' (primary), 'Conformal p-values as contamination priors for gated IRT' (secondary), 'RankLLM non-parametric ranking as sanity-check baseline for IRT-corrected rankings' (tertiary)",
  "approach": "We extend the Deterministic Gated IRT model (DGM; Shu et al., Psychometrika 2013) from the test-security domain to LLM contamination assessment, introducing the Gated-2PL (G-2PL) model as the primary framework where correct-response probability decomposes into ability-driven and contamination-driven components via a gating mechanism. The key innovation over DGM is that item exposure status is not assumed known but is identified from paired adversarial items.

**Model specification (primary: Gated-2PL):**
- For variant item i*: P(Y_{j,i*}=1 | θ_j) = σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i − δ_i)), a standard 2PL with difficulty shift δ_i
- For original item i: P(Y_{j,i}=1 | θ_j, ξ_j, η_i) = ξ_j·η_i + (1−ξ_j·η_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i))
- θ_j = model j's genuine reasoning ability (person parameter)
- ξ_j ∈ [0,1] = model j's contamination exposure (person parameter)
- η_i ∈ [0,1] = item i's contamination susceptibility (item parameter)
- a_i, b_i = discrimination and difficulty (shared across original-variant pairs)
- δ_i = variant difficulty shift (estimated from variant calibration)

**Rationale for G-2PL over G-3PL:** The guessing parameter c_i in 3PL requires 200+ examinees for stable estimation under classical methods, while we have only 15-20 models. Dropping c_i to use 2PL eliminates the most problematic parameter for small samples while retaining the core contamination decomposition. PSN-IRT succeeded with 12 models using neural estimation, but their 4PL worked because they had 41,871 items providing massive per-item information; our gated model adds M+K contamination parameters, making parsimony critical. For math benchmarks with open-ended answers (MATH-500, GSM8K), guessing probability is effectively zero, making 2PL substantively appropriate.

**Ablation to Gated-3PL (G-3PL):**
- P(Y_{j,i*}=1 | θ_j) = c_i + (1−c_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i − δ_i))
- P(Y_{j,i}=1 | θ_j, ξ_j, η_i) = ξ_j·η_i + (1−ξ_j·η_i)·[c_i + (1−c_i)·σ(a_i(θ_j − b_i))]
- c_i fixed to domain-specific constants: c_i = 0 for open-ended math (MATH-500, GSM8K), enabling estimation only for any future MCQ extensions.

**Estimation strategy (fully specified):**
Primary: Bayesian MCMC via NumPyro/Stan with hierarchical priors, following DGM's original estimation framework:
- θ_j ~ N(0, σ²_θ), σ_θ ~ Half-Cauchy(0, 2.5)
- ξ_j ~ Beta(α_ξ, β_ξ), with α_ξ, β_ξ ~ Gamma(2, 1) (hierarchical; allows posterior to concentrate near 0 for clean models or near 1 for heavily contaminated ones)
- η_i ~ Beta(α_η, β_η), with α_η, β_η ~ Gamma(2, 1) (hierarchical)
- a_i ~ LogNormal(0, 0.5) (positive discrimination, weakly informative)
- b_i ~ N(0, 1) (centered difficulty)
- δ_i ~ N(0, 0.5) (variant shifts expected small)
- MCMC: 4 chains × 2,000 warmup + 2,000 samples, NUTS sampler, R̂ < 1.05 convergence criterion
Comparison: Neural estimation extending PSN-IRT's pseudo-Siamese architecture with an additional gating head that outputs (ξ_j, η_i) — trained via binary cross-entropy on the joint original+variant response matrix. This provides a non-Bayesian point estimate comparison.
Ablation: Variational inference via Pyro SVI as a faster alternative to MCMC, using amortized inference for scalability testing.

**Formal identifiability (central theoretical contribution):**
We prove identifiability via a two-step argument: (1) Variant items serve as contamination-free anchors, identifying θ_j and item parameters {a_i, b_i} via standard 2PL identifiability conditions (≥2 items with heterogeneous discriminations; cf. Maris & Bechger 2009). The difficulty shift δ_i is estimated from the variant calibration. (2) Given identified θ_j and item parameters, the original-variant performance gap identifies the bilinear product ξ_j·η_i. Under the rank-1 bilinear decomposition ξ_j·η_i with M models and K items, we have M·K observed gaps constraining M+K−1 free parameters (one fixed for scale), identifiable when M·K > M+K−1, i.e., (M−1)(K−1) > 0. This holds for any M,K ≥ 2. The 2PL formulation avoids the flat-likelihood surfaces that plague 3PL/4PL estimation with few examinees, as the Fisher information matrix for the 2PL is well-conditioned even at M=15.

**Bilinear rank-1 model adequacy plan:**
The rank-1 assumption (ξ_j·η_i) treats contamination as model-global and item-global, which is a first-order approximation — in reality, contamination may be topic-dependent (e.g., a model contaminated on geometry but not algebra). We address this as follows:
(a) Compute standardized residuals r_{j,i} = (Y_{j,i} − P̂_{j,i}) / √(P̂_{j,i}(1−P̂_{j,i})) from the rank-1 fit and report the residual matrix.
(b) Compute Yen's Q3 statistic for local dependence among original items after conditioning on θ_j — systematic topic-structured residuals would indicate rank-1 insufficiency.
(c) Apply person-fit statistics (standardized log-likelihood lz*) to detect models whose original-item response patterns deviate from the G-2PL predictions, flagging potential topic-specific contamination.
(d) If structured residuals emerge, explore rank-2 extension (ξ_j·η_i → ξ_j^(1)·η_i^(1) + ξ_j^(2)·η_i^(2)) or topic-stratified estimation as explicit future work.
(e) Justification for rank-1 as starting point: LLM contamination is primarily driven by overall training data overlap (entire benchmark suites appearing in Common Crawl/web scrapes) rather than topic-selective memorization; the rank-1 model captures this dominant effect.

**Data collection (within 200 H100-hr budget):**
For ~1,000 items from MATH-500 and a GSM8K subset, we generate symbolically-verified adversarial variants. Primary pipeline: MaSTer-style multi-round rewrite-verify using Qwen3.6-27B as rewriter with SymPy answer verification (~25 H100-hrs). Backup (if MaSTer code unavailable by week 1): (a) single-round rewrite-verify pipeline with Qwen3.6-27B + SymPy checking, implementable in 2-3 days; (b) MathCheck (ICLR 2025, open code at github.com/PremiLab-Math/MathCheck) for GSM8K variants; (c) seed with MATH-Perturb's 279 expert-crafted perturbations (ICML 2025, open code at github.com/Kaffaljidhmah2/MATH-Perturb) and extend via LLM rewriting for remaining items. We collect response matrices from 15-20 models: 10 open-weight (DeepSeek-R2 32B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, GLM-5.1 754B-A40B, OLMo-2-13B, Llama-4-Maverick-17B-A400B, Mistral-Large-3, plus 2 smaller reference models) and 5-8 closed-API models (GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro). For originals, we reuse Open LLM Leaderboard per-item response data (available via HuggingFace API at huggingface.co/datasets/open-llm-leaderboard/results) where available, requiring new inference only for variant items and models not on the leaderboard (~80 H100-hrs for open-weight variant inference, ~60 H100-hrs for missing original runs). IRT fitting is negligible (<1 hr CPU for MCMC).

**Validation (three-pronged, addressing domain mismatch concern):**

(1) External ranking correlation: Kendall-τ of CRADE-corrected ability rankings vs. MathArena 2026 uncontaminated competition rankings (~900 problems, 50+ models), targeting τ ≥ 0.85 (revised from 0.90 given domain mismatch between textbook-style MATH-500/GSM8K and competition-style MathArena). Report bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Compare against: (a) raw accuracy rankings, (b) RankLLM difficulty-weighted rankings, (c) DCR-corrected rankings (r=0.66 on hard tasks), (d) JECS-filtered rankings.

(2) Synthetic contamination injection (causal validation): Deliberately fine-tune OLMo-2-13B on MATH-500 training items (1 epoch, mild contamination following established protocols from contamination survey literature) and re-evaluate. If G-2PL correctly recovers elevated ξ for the fine-tuned model while θ remains stable (matching pre-contamination ability), this provides causal evidence that the decomposition works. Compare fine-tuned ξ against clean OLMo-2-13B ξ via posterior credible interval separation. This is the strongest validation because it provides ground-truth contamination status.

(3) Convergent validity with existing detectors: Correlate G-2PL's per-model ξ_j estimates with: (a) ConStat contamination flags (performance gap on rephrased vs. original), (b) PaCoST binary contamination verdicts (paired confidence significance test), (c) PSN-IRT's anomalous guessing-rate parameters. High concordance validates that ξ captures the same construct; low concordance would require investigation of what ξ uniquely captures beyond existing methods.

(4) Ablation showing differential correction benefit: Demonstrate that CRADE correction improves ranking accuracy (vs. MathArena) more for models with high estimated ξ (provably or detectably contaminated) than for models with low ξ. This confirms the correction is targeted rather than uniformly applied.

**Anchor assumption validation (variant contamination-free):**
(a) Fit standard 2PL to variant-only response matrix and compute item-fit statistics (S-X² or Orlando-Thissen) and person-fit statistics (lz*). Good fit supports the anchor assumption — variants behave like clean IRT items measuring genuine ability.
(b) Check that variant difficulty b_i + δ_i is predictable from original difficulty b_i plus a systematic shift; high-residual outlier items may indicate re-contaminated variants and should be flagged for manual review.
(c) Cross-validation: Hold out 20% of variant items, fit 2PL on remaining 80%, predict held-out responses. Prediction accuracy comparable to full-data fit supports generalizability.
(d) Ablation: Compare CRADE results using MATH-Perturb's expert-crafted perturbations (strongest anchor assumption) vs. MaSTer/LLM-generated variants to assess sensitivity to variant quality.

Ablations: (a) G-2PL vs. G-3PL (with fixed c_i = 0 for math), (b) Bayesian MCMC vs. neural estimation vs. variational inference, (c) number of variant items (100/500/1000), (d) number of models (10/15/20), (e) sensitivity to variant difficulty shift δ_i, (f) rank-1 vs. rank-2 bilinear decomposition if residuals warrant it, (g) RankLLM vs. G-2PL ranking quality.",

## Research Findings

### 1. Growing Pains: Fixed-Parameter Calibration for LLM Evaluation

**Paper:** "Growing Pains: Extensible and Efficient LLM Benchmarking Via Fixed Parameter Calibration" (arXiv:2604.12843, April 2026) by Eliya Habba, Itay Itzhak, Asaf Yehudai, Yotam Perlitz, Elron Bandel, Michal Shmueli-Scheuer, Leshem Choshen, and Gabriel Stanovsky.

**Core Problem:** The rapid release of LLMs and benchmarks makes evaluating every model on every dataset increasingly costly. Models evaluated on different samples have incomparable scores.

**IRT Model Used:** Multidimensional 2-Parameter Logistic IRT (MIRT 2PL), which allows items to load on multiple latent dimensions. The literature suggests 3-8 interpretable skill dimensions underlie model performance, though the paper does not fix this parameter explicitly.

**Fixed-Parameter Calibration Procedure (Two Stages):**

- **Stage 1 (t=0):** Train initial MIRT 2PL model on the first dataset B0 using reference models. Estimate item parameters (discrimination `a` and difficulty `d`) for all items via maximum likelihood.
- **Stage 2 (t>0):** When a new benchmark Bt arrives, estimate its item parameters while **holding all existing anchor item parameters fixed**. Fit new item parameters using reference model responses to both new and existing anchor items, constraining anchor parameters to their previously calibrated values.

**Anchor Item Selection:** Items are selected by clustering the IRT item representations and selecting the most representative item from each cluster. This distributes anchors across difficulty and discrimination space rather than selecting only high-discrimination items.

**Quantitative Results:**
- **Prediction error:** 2-3 percentage points MAE
- **Ranking preservation:** Spearman rho >= 0.9
- **Anchor items needed:** 100 per dataset (tested 10, 25, 50, 100 -- diminishing returns below 100)
- **Models used:** Over 400 models total; 295 reference models for Open LLM Leaderboard (75% of 395), 321 for MMLU (75% of 428)
- **Minimum models needed:** ~100 models for stable results on OLL; ~25 reference models already yields robust performance on MMLU

**New Model Evaluation:** A new model's ability vector theta is estimated via maximum likelihood using only anchor responses. Then full-dataset performance is predicted by combining observed anchor responses with correctness probabilities from calibrated item parameters.

**Data Source:** Per-item response data from 395 LLMs on the Open LLM Leaderboard, sourced from Polo et al. (2024) -- the tinyBenchmarks work.

**Datasets Used (Open LLM Leaderboard v1):** ARC Challenge (1,212 items), GSM8K (1,359 items), HellaSwag (10,082 items), MMLU (14,042 items), TruthfulQA (857 items), Winogrande (1,307 items). Also tested on 57 MMLU subject subsets (100-1,534 items each).

---

### 2. Two-Stage IRT Fixed-Parameter Calibration Methodology

**General Methodology:**

1. **Stage 1 (Anchor Calibration):** Calibrate item parameters on a "base" test form using a sufficiently large reference sample. These parameters define the measurement scale.
2. **Stage 2 (New Item Calibration):** When new items are introduced, fix the anchor item parameters at their Stage 1 values. Estimate new item parameters and examinee abilities simultaneously, with the fixed anchors constraining the scale.

**Key Implementation Details:**
- The performance of FIPC (Fixed Item Parameter Calibration) depends critically on the MML estimation routine: best results come from **multiple updates of the prior latent ability distribution combined with multiple EM cycles** (the MWU-MEM method, per Kim 2020).
- Two methods for the bifactor model: OWU-MEM (one prior weights update, multiple EM cycles) and MWU-MEM (multiple prior weights updates, multiple EM cycles). MWU-MEM generally performs better.
- Fixed-b methods and two-stage methods show very high agreement (correlation ~0.999) in equating accuracy.

**For the LLM Context (Growing Pains):** The "examinees" are LLMs, not humans. Stage 1 calibrates item parameters using a large pool of reference models. Stage 2 handles new benchmarks or new models by fixing anchor parameters and estimating only the new unknowns.

---

### 3. Open LLM Leaderboard Per-Item Response Data on HuggingFace

There are **two different versions** with different URL structures:

**Version 1 (Archived -- the version used by Growing Pains/tinyBenchmarks):**
- URL pattern: `open-llm-leaderboard/details_{org}__{model_name}` (note: the org/model slash is replaced with double underscore)
- Example: `open-llm-leaderboard/details_meta-llama__Llama-2-70b-hf`
- Configurations named like: `harness_arc_challenge_25`, `harness_hellaswag_10`, `harness_winogrande_5`
- Load with: `load_dataset("open-llm-leaderboard/details_meta-llama__Llama-2-70b-hf", "harness_arc_challenge_25", split="train")`
- Per-item columns: `example`, `choices`, `gold`, `predictions`, `acc`, `acc_norm`, `id`
- Benchmarks: ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, Winogrande, GSM8K
- Archived datasets are under `open-llm-leaderboard-old/` namespace

**Version 2 (Current):**
- URL pattern: `open-llm-leaderboard/{org}__{model_name}-details`  (note the `-details` suffix, not `details_` prefix)
- Example: `open-llm-leaderboard/google__gemma-2-9b-details`
- Configurations named like: `google__gemma-2-9b__leaderboard_bbh_boolean_expressions`
- Load with: `load_dataset("open-llm-leaderboard/google__gemma-2-9b-details", name="google__gemma-2-9b__leaderboard_bbh_boolean_expressions", split="latest")`
- Split names: `latest`, `train` (alias), or timestamped splits like `"2024-08-07T12-52-38.325998"`
- 38 configurations per model covering: IFEval, BBH (23 subtasks), MATH Lvl 5 (8 subtasks), GPQA (3 subtasks), MuSR (3 subtasks), MMLU-PRO
- Per-task metrics vary: `acc_norm` for BBH/GPQA, `exact_match` for Math, `acc` for MMLU-PRO, multiple strict/loose accuracy metrics for IFEval
- Datasets are **gated** -- requires HuggingFace login and accepting terms
- The collection has 4,500+ items (one details dataset per evaluated model)
- Aggregate results: `open-llm-leaderboard/results` dataset and `open-llm-leaderboard/contents` dataset

**tinyBenchmarks (Polo et al., 2024):** The source data used by Growing Pains. Polo et al. collected per-item binary response data for 395 LLMs across ~29K items from the V1 leaderboard. They released tiny subsets (100 examples per benchmark) on HuggingFace. The full response matrix (395 models x 29K items) is what Growing Pains uses for its IRT calibration experiments.

---

### 4. Small-Sample IRT Calibration (N=15-20 Examinees in Stage 2)

This is the most challenging aspect of your use case. The literature provides the following guidance:

**Minimum Sample Size Recommendations (from Rasch/IRT literature):**
- For +/- 1 logit stability at 95% confidence: **16-36 examinees**
- For +/- 1 logit stability at 99% confidence: **27-61 examinees**
- Conservative recommendation: **50 well-targeted examinees**
- Minimum for well-designed pilots: **30 examinees**
- The formula SE ~ 2/sqrt(N) to 3/sqrt(N) governs how standard error decreases with sample size

**N=15-20 is below most minimum thresholds**, but the literature offers mitigation strategies:

**Best Estimation Methods for Very Small N:**
1. **Hierarchical Bayesian 2PL (OH2PL):** The optimized hierarchical Bayesian 2PL model produces unbiased item parameter estimates even at N=50. At N < 50, standard MML has 75-89% inadmissible solutions, while hierarchical Bayesian methods remain functional.
2. **Half-Cauchy or Exponential hyperpriors** on variance components yield the best results; avoid inverse Gamma priors.
3. **Partial pooling** (borrowing strength across items) is the key mechanism that makes hierarchical Bayesian approaches work with sparse data.

**Specific Recommendations for Your N=15-20 Scenario:**
- **Use fixed-parameter calibration rather than concurrent calibration.** Fix the item parameters from Stage 1 (calibrated on the large reference sample) and estimate only examinee abilities in Stage 2. This dramatically reduces the number of parameters to estimate.
- **With fixed item parameters, you are only estimating 15-20 ability vectors**, which is much more tractable than jointly estimating item + ability parameters.
- **Ensure sufficient item coverage:** At least 8 correct and 8 incorrect responses per item for stable calibration (Rasch recommendation). With only 15-20 examinees, very easy or very hard items will have unstable parameters.
- **Use Bayesian estimation with informative priors** derived from Stage 1 to regularize ability estimates.
- **The Growing Pains approach is encouraging for this scenario:** They show that with anchor items fixed from a large calibration, new models can be scored reliably. The key constraint is the number of anchor items (100 recommended), not the number of new models.
- **Increase sample sizes by 10-40%** when measurement disturbances exist (which they always do in LLM evaluation due to prompt sensitivity, temperature variation, etc.).

**Critical Caveat:** Most of the small-sample IRT literature deals with **item calibration** with few examinees. In the LLM context where you are estimating **model abilities** with fixed item parameters, the problem is actually more favorable -- you only need enough response data per model to estimate its ability vector reliably, which depends on the number of items each model answers (not the number of models). With 100 anchor items per dataset and fixed item parameters, estimating ability for even a single new model is feasible; the precision just depends on test length.

## Research Findings

### 1. Growing Pains: Fixed-Parameter Calibration for LLM Evaluation

**Paper:** "Growing Pains: Extensible and Efficient LLM Benchmarking Via Fixed Parameter Calibration" (arXiv:2604.12843, April 2026) by Eliya Habba, Itay Itzhak, Asaf Yehudai, Yotam Perlitz, Elron Bandel, Michal Shmueli-Scheuer, Leshem Choshen, and Gabriel Stanovsky.

**Core Problem:** The rapid release of LLMs and benchmarks makes evaluating every model on every dataset increasingly costly. Models evaluated on different samples have incomparable scores.

**IRT Model Used:** Multidimensional 2-Parameter Logistic IRT (MIRT 2PL), which allows items to load on multiple latent dimensions. The literature suggests 3-8 interpretable skill dimensions underlie model performance, though the paper does not fix this parameter explicitly.

**Fixed-Parameter Calibration Procedure (Two Stages):**

- **Stage 1 (t=0):** Train initial MIRT 2PL model on the first dataset B0 using reference models. Estimate item parameters (discrimination `a` and difficulty `d`) for all items via maximum likelihood.
- **Stage 2 (t>0):** When a new benchmark Bt arrives, estimate its item parameters while **holding all existing anchor item parameters fixed**. Fit new item parameters using reference model responses to both new and existing anchor items, constraining anchor parameters to their previously calibrated values.

**Anchor Item Selection:** Items are selected by clustering the IRT item representations and selecting the most representative item from each cluster. This distributes anchors across difficulty and discrimination space rather than selecting only high-discrimination items.

**Quantitative Results:**
- **Prediction error:** 2-3 percentage points MAE
- **Ranking preservation:** Spearman rho >= 0.9
- **Anchor items needed:** 100 per dataset (tested 10, 25, 50, 100 -- diminishing returns below 100)
- **Models used:** Over 400 models total; 295 reference models for Open LLM Leaderboard (75% of 395), 321 for MMLU (75% of 428)
- **Minimum models needed:** ~100 models for stable results on OLL; ~25 reference models already yields robust performance on MMLU

**New Model Evaluation:** A new model's ability vector theta is estimated via maximum likelihood using only anchor responses. Then full-dataset performance is predicted by combining observed anchor responses with correctness probabilities from calibrated item parameters.

**Data Source:** Per-item response data from 395 LLMs on the Open LLM Leaderboard, sourced from Polo et al. (2024) -- the tinyBenchmarks work.

**Datasets Used (Open LLM Leaderboard v1):** ARC Challenge (1,212 items), GSM8K (1,359 items), HellaSwag (10,082 items), MMLU (14,042 items), TruthfulQA (857 items), Winogrande (1,307 items). Also tested on 57 MMLU subject subsets (100-1,534 items each).

---

### 2. Two-Stage IRT Fixed-Parameter Calibration Methodology

**General Methodology:**

1. **Stage 1 (Anchor Calibration):** Calibrate item parameters on a "base" test form using a sufficiently large reference sample. These parameters define the measurement scale.
2. **Stage 2 (New Item Calibration):** When new items are introduced, fix the anchor item parameters at their Stage 1 values. Estimate new item parameters and examinee abilities simultaneously, with the fixed anchors constraining the scale.

**Key Implementation Details:**
- The performance of FIPC (Fixed Item Parameter Calibration) depends critically on the MML estimation routine: best results come from **multiple updates of the prior latent ability distribution combined with multiple EM cycles** (the MWU-MEM method, per Kim 2020).
- Two methods for the bifactor model: OWU-MEM (one prior weights update, multiple EM cycles) and MWU-MEM (multiple prior weights updates, multiple EM cycles). MWU-MEM generally performs better.
- Fixed-b methods and two-stage methods show very high agreement (correlation ~0.999) in equating accuracy.

**For the LLM Context (Growing Pains):** The "examinees" are LLMs, not humans. Stage 1 calibrates item parameters using a large pool of reference models. Stage 2 handles new benchmarks or new models by fixing anchor parameters and estimating only the new unknowns.

---

### 3. Open LLM Leaderboard Per-Item Response Data on HuggingFace

They released tiny subsets (100 examples per benchmark) on HuggingFace. The full response matrix (395 models x 29K items) is what Growing Pains uses for its IRT calibration experiments.

### 4. Small-Sample IRT Calibration (N=15-20 Examinees in Stage 2)

This is the most challenging aspect of your use case. The literature provides the following guidance:

**Minimum Sample Size Recommendations (from Rasch/IRT literature):**
- For +/- 1 logit stability at 95% confidence: **16-36 examinees**
- For +/- 1 logit stability at 99% confidence: **27-61 examinees**
- Conservative recommendation: **50 well-targeted examinees**
- Minimum for well-designed pilots: **30 examinees**
- The formula SE ~ 2/sqrt(N) to 3/sqrt(N) governs how standard error decreases with sample size

**N=15-20 is below most minimum thresholds**, but the literature offers mitigation strategies:

**Best Estimation Methods for Very Small N:**
1. **Hierarchical Bayesian 2PL (OH2PL):** The optimized hierarchical Bayesian 2PL model produces unbiased item parameter estimates even at N=50. At N < 50, standard MML has 75-89% inadmissible solutions, while hierarchical Bayesian methods remain functional.
2. **Half-Cauchy or Exponential hyperpriors** on variance components yield the best results; avoid inverse Gamma priors.
3. **Partial pooling** (borrowing strength across items) is the key mechanism that makes hierarchical Bayesian approaches work with sparse data.

**Specific Recommendations for Your N=15-20 Scenario:**
- **Use fixed-parameter calibration rather than concurrent calibration.** Fix the item parameters from Stage 1 (calibrated on the large reference sample) and estimate only examinee abilities in Stage 2. This dramatically reduces the number of parameters to estimate.
- **With fixed item parameters, you are only estimating 15-20 ability vectors**, which is much more tractable than jointly estimating item + ability parameters.
- **Ensure sufficient item coverage:** At least 8 correct and 8 incorrect responses per item for stable calibration (Rasch recommendation). With only 15-20 examinees, very easy or very hard items will have unstable parameters.
- **Use Bayesian estimation with informative priors** derived from Stage 1 to regularize ability estimates.
- **The Growing Pains approach is encouraging for this scenario:** They show that with anchor items fixed from a large calibration, new models can be scored reliably. The key constraint is the number of anchor items (100 recommended), not the number of new models.
- **Increase sample sizes by 10-40%** when measurement disturbances exist (which they always do in LLM evaluation due to prompt sensitivity, temperature variation, etc.).

**Critical Caveat:** Most of the small-sample IRT literature deals with **item calibration** with few examinees. In the LLM context where you are estimating **model abilities** with fixed item parameters, the problem is actually more favorable -- you only need enough response data per model to estimate its ability vector reliably, which depends on the number of items each model answers (not the number of models). With 100 anchor items per dataset and fixed item parameters, estimating ability for even a single new model is feasible; the precision just depends on test length.

## 1. Standard Simulation Study Designs for IRT Parameter Recovery

### Number of Replications

There is no single universally agreed number, but the literature converges on the following norms:

- **100 replications** is commonly cited as a working minimum for parameter recovery studies (Bulut simulation textbook; Konig et al. 2023 robustness study used 100 per condition across 864 conditions).
- **500 replications** is very common in the IRT literature and considered solid (the prior-sensitivity study by PMC11268390 used 500; mixed polytomous IRT studies used 500 per condition).
- **1,000 replications** is the gold standard used in the Fox (2025) JEBS paper for comparing IRT-BCSM to 2PL/2PNO models.
- **At least 625 replications** is the empirically derived recommendation from a guide published in the *International Journal of Assessment Tools in Education* for achieving accurate Type I error rate estimation in IRT models. A minimum of 156 is considered the absolute floor.
- Mundform et al. (JMASM) synthesized four studies and found that 5,000+ replications are rarely necessary; moderate numbers suffice.

**Practical recommendation**: For a novel IRT model validation, 500-1,000 replications is the range that will satisfy reviewers. Use 1,000 if computationally feasible.

### Standard Conditions to Vary (Fully Crossed Design)

Typical IRT simulation studies cross the following factors:

| Factor | Common Levels |
|--------|--------------|
| Sample size (N) | 3-6 levels spanning the range of interest |
| Test length (m) | 2-3 levels (e.g., 5, 10, 20, or 25, 50) |
| Item parameter distributions | 1-3 configurations |
| Model-specific parameters | Varies by model |
| Estimation method | 2-4 comparators |

This produces a fully crossed design. For example, Fox (2025) used N x m x tau = 4 x 2 x 5 = 40 cells with 1,000 replications each. Konig et al. (2023) used 864 total conditions with 100 replications each.

### Standard Metrics to Report

The following metrics are considered standard and expected by reviewers:

1. **Bias**: Mean(estimate - true value) averaged across replications. Should approach zero.
2. **RMSE**: sqrt(Mean((estimate - true value)^2)) averaged across replications. Captures both bias and variance.
3. **SD or SE of estimates**: Average posterior SD (Bayesian) or standard error (frequentist) across replications.
4. **95% Coverage rate**: Proportion of replications where the true value falls within the 95% credible/confidence interval. Should be near 0.95. This is especially important for Bayesian methods.
5. **Correlation**: Pearson or Spearman correlation between estimated and true parameters.

Additional metrics used in some studies:
- Root median squared error (RMdSE) -- robust to outlier estimates
- HDI width (Bayesian) -- measures precision
- Convergence rates / non-convergence rates
- Effective sample size (ESS) for MCMC
- Type I error and power (for classification-oriented models)

---

## 3. The Original DGM Paper: Shu, Henson, & Luecht (2013, Psychometrika)

**Citation**: Shu, Z., Henson, R., & Luecht, R. (2013). Using deterministic, gated item response theory model to detect test cheating due to item compromise. *Psychometrika*, 78(3), 481-497.

The full text is behind paywalls, but from the abstract, citing papers, and application studies, the following is established:

### The Gating Function

The DGM decomposes observed performance into two distributions using gating variables:
- **G_i**: Item exposure status (1 = compromised, 0 = secure)
- **T_m**: Student cheating status (1 = cheater, 0 = non-cheater), determined by whether theta_true < theta_cheat

The probability model conditions on both gates:
- For non-cheaters or secure items: P(Y=1) uses theta_true (standard IRT)
- For cheaters on compromised items: P(Y=1) uses theta_cheat (cheating ability)

This creates a deterministic "gate" that routes examinees through different IRT models depending on their cheating status and item compromise status.

### Estimation

Hierarchical MCMC is the estimation framework. The model is Bayesian throughout.

### Simulation Details (from Severo et al. 2019 application)

A paper applying the DGM to clinical anatomy exams (Severo et al., BMC Medical Education, 2019) provides the most detailed publicly accessible implementation:
- **MCMC**: 110,000 iterations, 10,000 burn-in, thinning every 100 iterations (keeping 1,000 posterior draws)
- **Real data**: ~200 students per exam, 100 items, 20 reused (compromised) items
- **Simulation for sensitivity/specificity**: 100 replicates, 200 students, 4 prevalence levels (5%, 10%, 35%, 70%), 2 efficacy levels
- **Results**: Specificity 68-98%, Sensitivity 60-91%

The original Shu et al. 2013 paper conducted two simulation studies to demonstrate parameter recovery. Based on summaries in citing works, these involved varying the proportion of cheaters and compromised items, with metrics including classification accuracy (sensitivity/specificity), Type I error rates, and power for detecting cheaters. The exact sample sizes and replication counts require access to the full paper, but the application literature suggests operational-scale sample sizes (hundreds to thousands of examinees) were used, consistent with the large-scale testing context the DGM was designed for.

---

## 4. Whether Fixed-Parameter Calibration Changes the Simulation Design

**The short answer is yes -- it substantially simplifies and changes the simulation design.**

### What Fixed-Parameter Calibration (FPC) Means

In FPC, item parameters (discrimination and difficulty) are treated as known and fixed to values calibrated from a prior large-N study. Only person-level parameters (abilities, classification variables, etc.) need to be estimated from the new (potentially small) sample.

### How This Changes Simulation Design

1. **Eliminates item parameter recovery as an evaluation target**: You no longer need to assess bias/RMSE of item discrimination and difficulty parameters, because they are not being estimated.

2. **Reduces the incidental parameter problem**: Fox (2025) explains that the incidental parameter problem in IRT arises because each new person introduces a new parameter. Fixing items removes half the parameter estimation burden. The IRT-BCSM goes further by integrating out person parameters entirely.

3. **Enables smaller sample sizes**: The literature consistently shows that when item parameters are fixed, much smaller samples suffice for person parameter estimation. The IRT-BCSM with fixed item parameters works at N=50 with m=5 items.

4. **Changes what you simulate**: Instead of generating item parameters per replication (or using fixed generating values and recovering them), you:
   - Fix item parameters to known values (from a real calibration or chosen generating values)
   - Generate person parameters and response data
   - Estimate only person-level quantities
   - Evaluate person parameter recovery (bias, RMSE, coverage of theta estimates)
   - For classification models like the DGM: evaluate classification accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC)

5. **Reduces conditions to vary**: You no longer need to cross item parameter distributions or test lengths (since items are fixed). Key factors become:
   - Sample size (N)
   - True parameter values for the novel components (e.g., cheating ability, gating probability)
   - Prevalence of the phenomenon being detected (e.g., proportion of cheaters)
   - Quality of the fixed item parameters (could add a condition with perturbed/noisy item params)

6. **Fox's IRT-BCSM explicitly uses this architecture**: The model consists of (fixed) item parameters and a common covariance parameter tau. Person parameters are post-hoc sampled. This is why it works at N=50.

### Simulation Design for a Novel Model with Fixed Item Parameters

Based on the literature reviewed, a recommended design would be:

| Design Element | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Replications | 500-1,000 |
| Sample sizes | N = 15, 25, 50, 100, 200 (covering your range of interest) |
| Items | Use realistic values from your application (e.g., 10, 20 items) |
| Item parameters | Fixed to calibrated values or realistic generating values |
| Person parameters | Generated from specified distributions |
| Novel model parameters | Vary across 3-5 levels of the key parameters |
| Metrics | Bias, RMSE, 95% CI/HDI coverage for person parameters; sensitivity/specificity/AUC for classification |
| MCMC details | Report iterations, burn-in, thinning, ESS, R-hat convergence diagnostic |
| Comparator models | At least one established model for baseline comparison |

---

## 5. Key Takeaways for Validating a Novel IRT Model

1. **Use 500-1,000 replications** per condition. 1,000 is the gold standard (Fox 2025), but 500 is acceptable and 100 is the minimum.

2. **Report bias, RMSE, SD/SE, and 95% coverage** as your core metrics. Add correlation between true and estimated values if relevant.

3. **N=50 is achievable** in Bayesian IRT with appropriate model reparameterization. Fox's IRT-BCSM and Konig's OH2PL both demonstrate this. N=15-25 would be pushing new ground -- be explicit about the exploratory nature.

4. **Fixed item parameters dramatically help small-sample estimation**. If your novel model can leverage previously calibrated item parameters, this is a major advantage and should be highlighted.

5. **Include a standard model as comparator** (e.g., 2PL with MML, standard Bayesian 2PNO) to show where established methods fail and your model succeeds at small N.

6. **For gated/classification models**, report classification metrics (sensitivity, specificity, false positive rate) in addition to parameter recovery metrics.

7. **MCMC diagnostics matter**: Report R-hat convergence, ESS, and note any non-convergence rates across conditions. Fox showed the IRT-BCSM maintained ESS > 400 at N=50 while the 2PNO collapsed.

8. **Prior sensitivity**: At small N, priors matter enormously. Consider a secondary simulation or sensitivity analysis varying prior specifications (Fox, Konig, and the PMC11268390 study all emphasize this).

Here is my detailed research report on IRT parameter recovery simulation study designs, with particular attention to small sample sizes and the DGM model.

---

## 1. Standard Simulation Study Designs for IRT Parameter Recovery

### Number of Replications

There is no single universally agreed number, but the literature converges on the following norms:

- **100 replications** is commonly cited as a working minimum for parameter recovery studies (Bulut simulation textbook; Konig et al. 2023 robustness study used 100 per condition across 864 conditions).
- **500 replications** is very common in the IRT literature and considered solid (the prior-sensitivity study by PMC11268390 used 500; mixed polytomous IRT studies used 500 per condition).
- **1,000 replications** is the gold standard used in the Fox (2025) JEBS paper for comparing IRT-BCSM to 2PL/2PNO models.
- **At least 625 replications** is the empirically derived recommendation from a guide published in the *International Journal of Assessment Tools in Education* for achieving accurate Type I error rate estimation in IRT models. A minimum of 156 is considered the absolute floor.
- Mundform et al. (JMASM) synthesized four studies and found that 5,000+ replications are rarely necessary; moderate numbers suffice.

**Practical recommendation**: For a novel IRT model validation, 500-1,000 replications is the range that will satisfy reviewers. Use 1,000 if computationally feasible.

### Standard Conditions to Vary (Fully Crossed Design)

Typical IRT simulation studies cross the following factors:

| Factor | Common Levels |
|--------|--------------|
| Sample size (N) | 3-6 levels spanning the range of interest |
| Test length (m) | 2-3 levels (e.g., 5, 10, 20, or 25, 50) |
| Item parameter distributions | 1-3 configurations |
| Model-specific parameters | Varies by model |
| Estimation method | 2-4 comparators |

This produces a fully crossed design. For example, Fox (2025) used N x m x tau = 4 x 2 x 5 = 40 cells with 1,000 replications each. Konig et al. (2023) used 864 total conditions with 100 replications each.

### Standard Metrics to Report

The following metrics are considered standard and expected by reviewers:

1. **Bias**: Mean(estimate - true value) averaged across replications. Should approach zero.
2. **RMSE**: sqrt(Mean((estimate - true value)^2)) averaged across replications. Captures both bias and variance.
3. **SD or SE of estimates**: Average posterior SD (Bayesian) or standard error (frequentist) across replications.
4. **95% Coverage rate**: Proportion of replications where the true value falls within the 95% credible/confidence interval. Should be near 0.95. This is especially important for Bayesian methods.
5. **Correlation**: Pearson or Spearman correlation between estimated and true parameters.

Additional metrics used in some studies:
- Root median squared error (RMdSE) -- robust to outlier estimates
- HDI width (Bayesian) -- measures precision
- Convergence rates / non-convergence rates
- Effective sample size (ESS) for MCMC
- Type I error and power (for classification-oriented models)

---

## 2. Small Sample Sizes Successfully Validated in Bayesian IRT

### Fox (2025) -- IRT-BCSM (JEBS, Vol. 50, No. 2, pp. 272-295)

This is the key reference for small-sample IRT. The paper's full simulation details from the PDF:

**Study 1: Model Comparison** (IRT-BCSM vs. 2PL vs. 2PNO)
- **Sample sizes**: N = 50, 100, 500, 1,000
- **Items**: m = 10
- **Replications**: 1,000 datasets per condition
- **Generating parameters**: Discrimination ~ N(0.80, 0.10), Difficulty ~ N(0, 0.50), latent variable variance fixed at 1
- **MCMC**: 6,000 total iterations, 1,000 burn-in, for the 2PNO (using R package `sirt`, function `mcmc.2pno`). The IRT-BCSM Gibbs sampler ran 5,000 iterations with burn-in of 500.
- **Metrics**: RMSE and SD, averaged across items and replications
- **Prior hyperparameters**: Shape g1 = 0.01, scale g2 = 0.01 for inverse-gamma priors on variance parameters

**Key Results from Table 1** (RMSE for discrimination, difficulty):
| N | IRT-BCSM (a, b) | 2PL/ML (a, b, d) | 2PNO/MCMC (a, b) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 0.056, 0.045 | 0.111, 0.092, 0.069 | 0.073, 0.045 |
| 500 | 0.067, 0.064 | 0.163, 0.140, 0.099 | 0.113, 0.067 |
| 100 | 0.109, 0.143 | 0.550, 37.82, 0.233 | 0.905, 0.260 |
| **50** | **0.110, 0.203** | **1.782, >100, 0.529** | **3.621, 1.101** |

At N=50, the 2PL (MML) and 2PNO (MCMC) completely broke down, with RMSEs of 1.782 and 3.621 for discrimination. The IRT-BCSM maintained an RMSE of only 0.110 for discrimination and 0.203 for difficulty -- remaining usable.

**Study 2: Parameter Recovery of IRT-BCSM Specifically**
- **Sample sizes**: N = 50, 100, 500
- **Items**: m = 5 and m = 10
- **Replications**: 1,000
- **Common covariance tau varied**: 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.80, 1.00
- **Metrics**: RMSE plotted across tau values and sample sizes (Figure 1)
- Discrimination RMSE at small samples converged to ~0.25 (the SD of the generating distribution), showing the estimates are at least as good as the prior.
- Difficulty RMSE remained below 0.40 even at N=50 with m=5.

**Table 3** showed tau recovery: At N=50, m=5, binary data, the posterior mean/median of tau was close to the true value across all conditions (0.00 to 1.00), though posterior SDs were larger (0.07-0.84).

**MCMC Efficiency (Table 2)**: The IRT-BCSM maintained high effective sample sizes even at N=50 (mean ESS ~1,462 for discrimination, ~1,764 for difficulty). The 2PNO collapsed to mean ESS of ~167 for discrimination at N=50.

### Konig et al. (2020, 2023) -- Optimized Hierarchical 2PL

**Konig et al. (2020)** original paper: N=100 was the smallest tested; showed the OH2PL yielded accurate estimates there.

**Konig et al. (2023) robustness study** (Behavior Research Methods, PMC10700496):
- **Sample sizes**: N = 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 500
- **Items**: k = 25 and k = 50
- **Replications**: 100 per condition
- **Conditions**: 864 total (6 sample sizes x 2 test lengths x 3 variance component levels x 2 correlations x 4 hyperprior specs x 3 hyperprior distributions)
- **MCMC**: Stan via RStan, 3 chains x 4,000 iterations with 1,000 burn-in. Convergence: R-hat < 1.05.
- **Metrics**: Bias, RMSE, 95% HDI coverage
- **Key result at N=50**: The OH2PL with half-Cauchy or Exponential hyperpriors yielded unbiased estimates. Bias for difficulty remained within +/- 0.04 across all conditions. Person parameter bias was between +/- 0.03. MML showed 75-89% inadmissible solutions at N=50 under extreme variance conditions.

### Prior Distribution Studies

**Bayesian Prior Choice (Frontiers, PMC5037236)**:
- Tested N = 250, 500, 1,000, 2,000 with 100 replications each
- Compared MCMC (OpenBUGS, 5,000 burn-in + 1,000 post) vs. VB (Infer.NET)
- At N=250, vague priors produced large errors; hierarchical and matched priors performed well
- Recommendation: Use hierarchical priors when true distributions are unknown

**Prior Sensitivity Study (PMC11268390)**:
- N = 100, 500, 1,000 with 500 replications, 45 items
- At N=100, 100% of replications had estimation problems without priors
- Priors on both a and c parameters were needed for N=100
- Mismatched prior modes caused substantial bias even with weakly informative priors

### Graded Response Model (MML vs. MCMC)

- Tested N = 75 and 150 (among others)
- MCMC (Gibbs sampling) recovered some threshold parameters better than MML at N=75 and N=150
- Little difference above N=300

---

## 3. The Original DGM Paper: Shu, Henson, & Luecht (2013, Psychometrika)

**Citation**: Shu, Z., Henson, R., & Luecht, R. (2013). Using deterministic, gated item response theory model to detect test cheating due to item compromise. *Psychometrika*, 78(3), 481-497.

The full text is behind paywalls, but from the abstract, citing papers, and application studies, the following is established:

### The Gating Function

The DGM decomposes observed performance into two distributions using gating variables:
- **G_i**: Item exposure status (1 = compromised, 0 = secure)
- **T_m**: Student cheating status (1 = cheater, 0 = non-cheater), determined by whether theta_true < theta_cheat

The probability model conditions on both gates:
- For non-cheaters or secure items: P(Y=1) uses theta_true (standard IRT)
- For cheaters on compromised items: P(Y=1) uses theta_cheat (cheating ability)

This creates a deterministic "gate" that routes examinees through different IRT models depending on their cheating status and item compromise status.

### Estimation

Hierarchical MCMC is the estimation framework. The model is Bayesian throughout.

### Simulation Details (from Severo et al. 2019 application)

A paper applying the DGM to clinical anatomy exams (Severo et al., BMC Medical Education, 2019) provides the most detailed publicly accessible implementation:
- **MCMC**: 110,000 iterations, 10,000 burn-in, thinning every 100 iterations (keeping 1,000 posterior draws)
- **Real data**: ~200 students per exam, 100 items, 20 reused (compromised) items
- **Simulation for sensitivity/specificity**: 100 replicates, 200 students, 4 prevalence levels (5%, 10%, 35%, 70%), 2 efficacy levels
- **Results**: Specificity 68-98%, Sensitivity 60-91%

The original Shu et al. 2013 paper conducted two simulation studies to demonstrate parameter recovery. Based on summaries in citing works, these involved varying the proportion of cheaters and compromised items, with metrics including classification accuracy (sensitivity/specificity), Type I error rates, and power for detecting cheaters. The exact sample sizes and replication counts require access to the full paper, but the application literature suggests operational-scale sample sizes (hundreds to thousands of examinees) were used, consistent with the large-scale testing context the DGM was designed for.

---

## 4. Whether Fixed-Parameter Calibration Changes the Simulation Design

**The short answer is yes -- it substantially simplifies and changes the simulation design.**

### What Fixed-Parameter Calibration (FPC) Means

In FPC, item parameters (discrimination and difficulty) are treated as known and fixed to values calibrated from a prior large-N study. Only person-level parameters (abilities, classification variables, etc.) need to be estimated from the new (potentially small) sample.

### How This Changes Simulation Design

1. **Eliminates item parameter recovery as an evaluation target**: You no longer need to assess bias/RMSE of item discrimination and difficulty parameters, because they are not being estimated.

2. **Reduces the incidental parameter problem**: Fox (2025) explains that the incidental parameter problem in IRT arises because each new person introduces a new parameter. Fixing items removes half the parameter estimation burden. The IRT-BCSM goes further by integrating out person parameters entirely.

3. **Enables smaller sample sizes**: The literature consistently shows that when item parameters are fixed, much smaller samples suffice for person parameter estimation. The IRT-BCSM with fixed item parameters works at N=50 with m=5 items.

4. **Changes what you simulate**: Instead of generating item parameters per replication (or using fixed generating values and recovering them), you:
   - Fix item parameters to known values (from a real calibration or chosen generating values)
   - Generate person parameters and response data
   - Estimate only person-level quantities
   - Evaluate person parameter recovery (bias, RMSE, coverage of theta estimates)
   - For classification models like the DGM: evaluate classification accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC)

5. **Reduces conditions to vary**: You no longer need to cross item parameter distributions or test lengths (since items are fixed). Key factors become:
   - Sample size (N)
   - True parameter values for the novel components (e.g., cheating ability, gating probability)
   - Prevalence of the phenomenon being detected (e.g., proportion of cheaters)
   - Quality of the fixed item parameters (could add a condition with perturbed/noisy item params)

6. **Fox's IRT-BCSM explicitly uses this architecture**: The model consists of (fixed) item parameters and a common covariance parameter tau. Person parameters are post-hoc sampled. This is why it works at N=50.

### Simulation Design for a Novel Model with Fixed Item Parameters

Based on the literature reviewed, a recommended design would be:

| Design Element | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Replications | 500-1,000 |
| Sample sizes | N = 15, 25, 50, 100, 200 (covering your range of interest) |
| Items | Use realistic values from your application (e.g., 10, 20 items) |
| Item parameters | Fixed to calibrated values or realistic generating values |
| Person parameters | Generated from specified distributions |
| Novel model parameters | Vary across 3-5 levels of the key parameters |
| Metrics | Bias, RMSE, 95% CI/HDI coverage for person parameters; sensitivity/specificity/AUC for classification |
| MCMC details | Report iterations, burn-in, thinning, ESS, R-hat convergence diagnostic |
| Comparator models | At least one established model for baseline comparison |

---

## 5. Key Takeaways for Validating a Novel IRT Model

1. **Use 500-1,000 replications** per condition. 1,000 is the gold standard (Fox 2025), but 500 is acceptable and 100 is the minimum.

2. **Report bias, RMSE, SD/SE, and 95% coverage** as your core metrics. Add correlation between true and estimated values if relevant.

3. **N=50 is achievable** in Bayesian IRT with appropriate model reparameterization. Fox's IRT-BCSM and Konig's OH2PL both demonstrate this. N=15-25 would be pushing new ground -- be explicit about the exploratory nature.

4. **Fixed item parameters dramatically help small-sample estimation**. If your novel model can leverage previously calibrated item parameters, this is a major advantage and should be highlighted.

5. **Include a standard model as comparator** (e.g., 2PL with MML, standard Bayesian 2PNO) to show where established methods fail and your model succeeds at small N.

6. **For gated/classification models**, report classification metrics (sensitivity, specificity, false positive rate) in addition to parameter recovery metrics.

7. **MCMC diagnostics matter**: Report R-hat convergence, ESS, and note any non-convergence rates across conditions. Fox showed the IRT-BCSM maintained ESS > 400 at N=50 while the 2PNO collapsed.

8. **Prior sensitivity**: At small N, priors matter enormously. Consider a secondary simulation or sensitivity analysis varying prior specifications (Fox, Konig, and the PMC11268390 study all emphasize this).

---
